HyDE stands for Hypothetical Document Embeddings and is a query expansion technique for dense retrieval. The core insight is that a question and a passage answering that question look very different in embedding space, even if they are semantically related. HyDE addresses this by using a language model to generate a hypothetical passage that would answer the query, then embedding that hypothetical passage instead of the raw query. The hypothesis is that a generated answer looks more like a real answer chunk in embedding space than the question does. At retrieval time, the hypothetical passage is embedded and used to search the vector database. The retrieved chunks are then passed to the language model along with the original query to generate the final answer. HyDE was introduced by Gao et al. in 2022 and has been shown to improve retrieval performance, particularly for queries where the question and answer use different vocabulary.
Hallucination in large language models refers to the generation of content that is factually incorrect, unsupported, or fabricated, despite appearing fluent and confident. Hallucinations arise because language models are trained to generate plausible next tokens based on patterns in training data, not to verify factual accuracy. There are two main types: intrinsic hallucination, where the model contradicts information present in the input context, and extrinsic hallucination, where the model generates information that cannot be verified from the context at all. RAG systems reduce hallucination by grounding generation in retrieved context, but do not eliminate it — models can still ignore the context or confabulate details. Evaluation of hallucination typically uses LLM-as-judge approaches, where a separate model is prompted to verify whether each claim in the generated answer is supported by the source context. Metrics include hallucination rate (fraction of answers containing unsupported claims) and faithfulness score (fraction of claims that are supported).
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines a retrieval system with a generative language model. The retrieval system fetches relevant documents from an external corpus given a query. These documents are then provided as context to the language model, which generates an answer grounded in the retrieved content. RAG was introduced by Lewis et al. in 2020 and addresses a key limitation of parametric language models: their knowledge is frozen at training time. RAG allows models to access up-to-date or domain-specific information without retraining. The retrieval component can use sparse methods like BM25, dense methods like embedding similarity, or hybrid approaches combining both. The quality of the final answer depends heavily on the quality of retrieval — if the wrong documents are fetched, the model generates answers based on irrelevant context. Evaluation of RAG systems therefore requires separate assessment of retrieval quality and generation quality.
Word embeddings are dense vector representations of words in a continuous vector space. Early embedding models like Word2Vec and GloVe produced static embeddings — each word had a single fixed vector regardless of context. The limitation was that polysemous words like "bank" had one vector regardless of whether it meant a river bank or a financial institution. Contextual embeddings, introduced by ELMo and later BERT, produce different vectors for the same word depending on its surrounding context. Sentence embeddings extend this idea to entire sentences or passages. Models like sentence-transformers produce fixed-size vectors for arbitrary-length text, optimized so that semantically similar texts produce nearby vectors. Cosine similarity is typically used to measure distance between embedding vectors. Embedding quality is evaluated on benchmarks like STS (Semantic Textual Similarity) which tests whether the model assigns higher similarity to more semantically related pairs.
Evaluation of information retrieval systems uses several standard metrics. Precision at K measures the fraction of retrieved documents in the top K positions that are relevant. Recall at K measures the fraction of all relevant documents that appear in the top K positions. Mean Average Precision (MAP) computes the mean of average precision scores across queries, where average precision is the area under the precision-recall curve. Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) accounts for graded relevance and penalizes relevant documents that appear lower in the ranking. For RAG systems, retrieval metrics are complemented by generation metrics. Faithfulness measures whether the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context. Answer relevance measures whether the generated answer addresses the question. Hallucination rate measures the fraction of claims in the generated answer that cannot be attributed to the retrieved context. Statistical significance testing using paired t-tests is used to determine whether observed differences between retrieval strategies are real or due to chance.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that combines information retrieval with language model generation.
Instead of relying solely on the model's parametric knowledge, RAG fetches relevant documents from an external corpus and uses them as context.
This approach reduces hallucinations and allows the model to answer questions about documents it was never trained on.
The retrieval step typically uses embedding-based semantic search, keyword search like BM25, or a hybrid of both.
Cross-encoder rerankers then reorder the retrieved results for better precision before passing them to the language model.
Cross-encoders are a class of neural models used for relevance scoring in information retrieval. Unlike bi-encoders which embed the query and document separately and compare their vectors, a cross-encoder takes the query and document concatenated as a single input and produces a relevance score directly. This joint encoding allows the model to model fine-grained interactions between query and document tokens through attention, leading to significantly higher accuracy than bi-encoder similarity. The tradeoff is speed: a cross-encoder must run inference for every query-document pair, making it impractical for first-stage retrieval over large corpora. Cross-encoders are therefore used as rerankers: a fast first-stage retriever (BM25 or ANN) fetches the top N candidates, and the cross-encoder reranks them to select the top K. The ms-marco-MiniLM family of cross-encoders from sentence-transformers is a popular choice for reranking in RAG pipelines, trained on the MS MARCO passage retrieval dataset.
BM25, which stands for Best Match 25, is a probabilistic ranking function used in information retrieval. It is an improvement over the TF-IDF weighting scheme and is the standard baseline in sparse retrieval. BM25 scores documents based on the frequency of query terms within the document, the length of the document relative to the average document length in the corpus, and two tunable parameters k1 and b. The parameter k1 controls term frequency saturation — how much repeated occurrences of a term increase the score. The parameter b controls document length normalization — how much longer documents are penalized. BM25 is computationally efficient because it builds an inverted index at indexing time and scores only documents containing at least one query term. It excels at exact keyword matching but fails to capture semantic similarity — it cannot match "cardiac arrest" with "heart attack" unless those exact terms appear together.
Chunking is the process of splitting documents into smaller passages for indexing in a RAG system. The choice of chunking strategy significantly affects retrieval quality. Fixed-size chunking splits text into segments of a fixed number of tokens, with optional overlap between adjacent chunks to avoid losing context at boundaries. Sentence-aware chunking splits at sentence boundaries to avoid cutting sentences in half. Recursive character splitting tries multiple separators in order (paragraphs, then sentences, then words) to produce chunks of the target size. Semantic chunking uses embedding similarity to split at points where the topic changes. The chunk size involves a tradeoff: smaller chunks have higher precision (more focused content per chunk) but lower recall (relevant information may span multiple chunks). Larger chunks have higher recall but may introduce noise by including irrelevant content. Typical chunk sizes range from 128 to 512 tokens. Overlap of 10-20% of the chunk size is common practice.
The Transformer architecture was introduced in the paper "Attention Is All You Need" by Vaswani et al. in 2017. It replaced recurrent neural networks as the dominant architecture for sequence-to-sequence tasks. The core innovation is the self-attention mechanism, which allows the model to weigh the relevance of each token in a sequence against every other token simultaneously. Unlike RNNs, Transformers process all tokens in parallel, making them significantly faster to train on modern hardware. The architecture consists of an encoder stack and a decoder stack, each made up of multiple identical layers. Each layer contains a multi-head self-attention sublayer and a position-wise feed-forward sublayer. Residual connections and layer normalization are applied around each sublayer. Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings to give the model information about token order, since self-attention itself is permutation-invariant.
Vector databases are purpose-built systems for storing and querying high-dimensional vectors. Unlike traditional databases that retrieve rows by exact key match or range queries, vector databases retrieve by approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search — finding vectors closest to a query vector in the embedding space. Common ANN algorithms include HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs), IVF (Inverted File Index), and PQ (Product Quantization). HNSW builds a multi-layer graph structure that allows logarithmic-time approximate nearest neighbor search. Popular vector databases include Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and Chroma. Chroma is an open-source, embedded vector database suitable for local development. It supports persistence to disk, metadata filtering, and multiple distance metrics including cosine, L2, and inner product. Vector databases are the core infrastructure component of RAG systems, semantic search engines, and recommendation systems.
